shut.text: The east stair door. Oak gone grey, three iron bands, and open a hand's width, as if whoever went through last was in too much of a hurry to pull it to. Or meant to come straight back.
Wind comes down through the gap, out of the dark inside. It smells of cold ash and candle-ends, and it doesn't stop.
You put your hand on the door to push it wider, and find you've stopped on the threshold, counting under your breath.
And you can't think what comes after one. You know it. You've known it all your life. It won't come.
The taper in your satchel is cold against your side. A taper's for the stair, Aldous said. You'll know which stair.
You take your hand off the door. Not yet. Your feet seem very sure about it.

choir.text: The east stair door, open its hand's width on the dark. Wind comes down through the gap, cold ash and candle-ends, the same as ever.
With Oriel sat still on her stone there's nothing on the crown to hear but the wind. And under the wind, coming down the stair, something else.

Her feet go by behind you on the path and on round, and while she's the far side of the Spire there's nothing on the crown to hear but the wind. And under the wind, coming down the stair, something else.

Singing. Not a tune: a great many voices, a long way up, all at the one thing and none of them getting to the end of it. The Quiet House at night. The Low Water, the night Hild rowed you out to the rock.
One voice is nearer than the rest. A woman's, a turn or two above the door, tired, as if she's been at it longer than any of them.
Iver said that, on his rock. One nearer than the rest. Some nights she nearly gets a word out.
Somebody told you about her once, on a rock in the Low Water. He doesn't know he did.

own.text: You take it out and hold it in the gap, in the wind off the stair.
The nearest voice stops. Not trailing off: stopped, the way somebody stops when a door opens on them. The rest go on without her.
For a long moment she doesn't start again. It is very like being looked at, from a turn above.
You put it away. After a while, from the beginning, she starts again.

listen.text: You stand with your hand on the cold oak and listen. She comes round to the place where she always stops, and this time she doesn't stop.
Two words, clear, down the dark, in a voice that's used to being listened to:
Then the singing closes over her again, and she's back at the beginning.
You find you've stopped on the threshold, counting under your breath. One. And nothing after one. Not yet.
There's a woman singing on that stair. I've never heard her in my life.
...I know when she'll breathe. How would I know that?

again.text: The door, its hand's width open on the dark. She's still singing, a turn or two up, and getting to the place where she stops.
'Not Hushed.' She doesn't get it out again. Once in three hundred years might be all she has.
The Provost is on the niche step, with her head turned to the door.

answer.text: The door, its hand's width open on the dark. She's singing, a turn or two up, and getting to the place where she stops.

The Provost comes up out of the dark under the warden's seat with the Long Book open along her arm and the pen in her other hand, and stands beside you. She doesn't say anything. She's waiting for you.

choice.text: Say her name up the stair. "Isolde Vane."
Write her in the Long Book, Provost. Not with the Hushed. As she was.
Let her sing. She's nearly got it out herself.

named.text: You say it into the gap, not loud. Isolde Vane.
Then, down the stair, one word, as if she's leaning over a rail a turn above you:
And she doesn't start again. The rest go on singing a long way up, a little thinner, with a gap in them the shape of one voice.
Three hundred years she wanted that. And we had it in a book.
I'd not have known you could say a thing like that to a stair. I'd have written it down.

written.text: She writes it standing, the book along her arm, the way the Long Book's written: a line, plain. Isolde Vane. Wakebearer. Not Hushed. Given to the flame awake, by the chapter's word, for asking.
Then she finds the old line every novice learns, the ember that walked her home, and strikes it through. Once, straight, so you can still read it. Struck, not scraped.
There. Anybody who opens it will know what we said. And that we said it.
Up the stair the nearest voice gets to the place where she stops, and stops, and goes back to the beginning. Written down isn't the same as told. But it can't be scraped.

left.text: She's been three hundred years at it. It's hers to get out.
The Provost shuts the Long Book on her finger, keeping the place. Up the stair the nearest voice comes round to where she stops, and stops, and starts again.
A little further, this time? You can't tell. You'd like to think so.

after.text: The east stair door, open its hand's width on the dark.
The singing comes down from a long way up, with a gap in it the shape of one voice.
She's still at it, a turn or two up. In the Long Book she's written down as she was. She doesn't know.
She's still at it, a turn or two up. Nearer, you'd swear, than yesterday.
You find you've stopped on the threshold, counting. One. And nothing after one.
The taper in your satchel was cut for this stair, a notch to a landing. A taper's for the stair, Aldous said. You know which stair now.
The ember is warm in your hand. It's walked you up every stair on the ring. It could walk you up this one, in the dark.

choice.text: Light the Stair-Taper from the ember, and go up.
Go up in the dark, counting.

climb.text: You take the Stair-Taper out and hold its wick to the ember, low, under your cupped hand, out of the wind. It catches the way the cressets caught: as if it had only been waiting to be asked.
You put your hand flat on the door and push. It goes, after three months, without a sound.
The hand goes up. The chapter stays at the foot. That's how it was always done, and for once I can see why.
I'll count you. Keepers count the hand up and the hand down. Go on.

The stair turns always to the left, inside the Spire's wall. Pale stone, worn into a dip in the middle of every step. The wind comes down past you, cold ash and candle-ends, and the taper leans from it and doesn't go out.

The stair turns always to the left, inside the Spire's wall. Pale stone, worn into a dip in the middle of every step. The wind comes down past you, cold ash and candle-ends. The ember shows you a step at a time and no more.
A landing: a flat place, a slit of grey in the outer wall. Your thumb finds the first notch in the taper as the flame comes level with it.
A landing: a flat place, a slit of grey in the outer wall.
One.
And then, as easy as breathing out: two. It was only ever waiting for the stair.
At the second turn the cold stands still in one place, about the size of somebody leaning on a rail. Nobody's singing in it. The rest of the singing goes on far above, round the gap.
You say 'Isolde' going by, not loud. Nothing answers. It doesn't need to.

At the second turn she's there: the nearest voice, close enough to touch, singing to the stair. As the taper comes round the turn she stops, the way she stops for your things, and you go by her in the quiet. Written down in the Long Book. She doesn't know.
At the second turn she's there, the nearest voice, close enough to touch. She comes round to the place where she stops, and doesn't stop.
'Not Hushed. Awake. I asked them.'
And then, lower, the way you'd speak to somebody passing on a stair: 'Somebody went down this way not long ago. Counting. With a coal.'
She doesn't sing again while you're on the stair. You can feel her listening to you go up.

Three. The flame burns down past the third notch, and you know, the way you know your own hand, that novices go up to the third landing and no further. Past the third. You went higher than you were told.
Three. You know, the way you know your own hand, that novices go up to the third landing and no further. You went higher than you were told.
Four. Five. Your feet know the dips in the steps before the light finds them. Six.
Far below, so faint it could be the wind, the Provost's voice: 'Six.' She's been counting with you all the way.
Far below, so faint it could be the wind, the Provost's voice: 'Six.' She's been counting with you all the way. And somewhere out on the crown, round and round, a woman's feet keeping time.
The singing is close above you now, a great many voices behind a door at the top of the stair. The stair turns once more.

after_up.text: The east stair door, pushed wide now, the way you left it. The wind still comes down, but it comes down past you, not at you.
You stand on the threshold and count up it without meaning to, all the way to seven, and stop. It doesn't hurt to.

choice.text: Go up to the last landing.

up_again.text: Seven landings, turning always to the left. You don't need a light for it. You never did.
Oriel Sayre comes in behind you, a step down, and stays a step down all the way. She carries nothing.
At the second turn the cold stands still, where somebody leans on a rail and doesn't sing.
At the second turn she stops singing to let you by.
